sim.fast_forward_hint: Long-run fast-forward: compress each step into one brief (one LLM call per agent per step), skipping the intra-day tick loop; state/goals/relationships still evolve approximately. How much time a step covers is set by Step unit next to it — Day suits 60/600-day horizons, Month or Year are what make multi-year runs feasible.
sim.step_unit_hint: How much time one fast-forward step covers: a day (one brief per agent per day), a month, or a year. Multi-year horizons need month or year — otherwise the call count grows linearly with the number of days. Only applies in fast-forward mode.
sim.randomness_hint: Randomness: higher means more frequent sudden (burst) events and larger day-to-day swings during fast-forward. 0 = fully deterministic (no bursts, no jitter). Only applies in fast-forward mode.
sim.routine_randomness_hint: Routine randomness: higher means agents follow their daily routine less — deviating from scheduled activities and their plan more often. 0 = strictly follow the schedule (sleep slots are unaffected).
sim.scheduled: Scheduled: the run starts automatically at {at}
btn.schedule_run_hint: Schedule a run: at the time you set, the server starts the simulation with the current config. The time is the local clock of the machine running the dashboard, and closing this page does not cancel it.

worlds.setup_hint: These settings are identical across every parallel world: same residents, same number of days, same random seed. Keeping them fixed is what lets you attribute the final differences to the event itself.
worlds.sub: Every world shares the same residents, the same random seed, and the same model. The only difference is what happened. Whatever diverges is what that event caused.

set.tab_env_help: Secrets and runtime switches. This only shows whether something is set and which one it is (keys masked); nothing is echoed back or edited here — edit the .env file at the repository root.
set.tab_files_help: The override layers as written: dashboard_config.json is what this panel writes, environment_config.json sits last in the chain.
set.pt_ollama_note: A local Ollama service. The address ends at /api/generate, and the model name must match `ollama list` exactly.
set.pt_openai_note: Anything speaking the OpenAI API: OpenAI itself, vLLM, LM Studio, omlx. The address ends at /v1 — no /chat/completions.
set.pt_anthropic_note: The Anthropic Messages API; MiniMax's anthropic endpoint counts too. Leave off /v1/messages — the code appends it.
set.warn_env_file: ⚠ data/environment_config.json overrides this last, so changing it here has no effect.
set.warn_env: ⚠ The GAWORLD_CONFIG_OVERRIDES environment variable overrides this, ahead of this panel.
set.warn_readonly: 🔒 Read-only: this model backend holds a plaintext key, so it is not editable in the browser.
set.not_json: The server did not return JSON (HTTP {status})
set.revert_title: Remove this key from dashboard_config.json and fall back to the code default
set.pick_help: Every task that does not name its own backend uses this one, so it drives almost all of the cost. Your choice only reaches dashboard_config.json when you press “Save Config” at the bottom right, and applies to the next run you start. To give an individual task a different backend, see llm → routing → tasks below.
set.pick_hint: Changes go to “Pending changes” on the right; press “Save Config” to apply them.
set.provider_list_help: “Test connection” really does send one very short generation request to the backend — only a real call tells “reachable” apart from “reachable but the model was never pulled / the key was rejected / it returns reasoning and no text”. It changes no configuration.
set.field_name_help: The name you refer to this backend by in the config, and the one shown in the dropdown above. Letters, digits, underscores and hyphens only.
set.field_model_help: The model identifier the backend itself knows, matching the server exactly. Get it wrong and “Test connection” will say so.
set.field_endpoint_help: Leave blank to use the default: {endpoint}
set.field_key_env_help: Give the *name* of the environment variable, not the key itself. dashboard_config.json is committed, so plaintext keys are not accepted here. Put the value in .env at the repository root and restart the simulation process; the “Environment” tab shows whether it was picked up.
set.field_timeout_help: How long one call may take. Local models are slow and usually need 600; 120 is plenty for cloud. Blank uses the code default.
set.add_card_help: The new backend is written into llm.providers in dashboard_config.json, appears in the dropdown above immediately, and is usable from the next run. Only environment-variable names are accepted, never plaintext keys.
set.add_card_title: Add a local or cloud model
set.section_empty: Nothing to show in this section.
set.env_is_secret: This is a secret; only the masked head and tail are shown, enough to tell which key is loaded.
set.env_not_secret: Not a secret — the full value is shown.
set.env_edit_note: To change it, edit .env at the repository root and restart the simulation process.
set.env_intro: These are read from .env by gaworld.env_loader when the process starts. This panel is read-only: secrets are masked, and changes go in the file itself. A restart of the simulation process is needed for them to take effect.
set.file_dashboard_note: This is the file this panel saves to. It deep-merges over the code defaults; “restore default” deletes the key from here rather than writing the default back — writing it back would pin it, and later changes to the code default would stop applying.
set.file_env_note: Configuration for the environment generator. It applies last in the override chain, so any key it sets wins over both dashboard_config.json and the environment variables. Only four keys are allowed: environment / external_environment / external_environment_service / environment_server.
set.no_pending: No changes yet. Anything you edit is listed here to check before saving.
set.pending_help: Changes stay in the browser until you press “Save Config”, which writes them to dashboard_config.json. Saving only affects the next run you start — it does not interrupt one already going.
set.overrides_help: How many settings differ from the code default, and which layer each one comes from. Anything shadowed by environment_config.json or an environment variable cannot be changed from this panel.
set.overrides_stat: {overridden} overridden, {shadowed} of them from a layer this panel cannot reach.
set.reset_all_hint: “Clear all overrides” empties dashboard_config.json and returns every setting to its code default. Environment variables and environment_config.json are untouched.
set.fix_json_first: Some JSON is malformed — fix it before saving.
set.dropped_n: dropped {count} (wrong type or no such key)
set.applies_next_run: . The changes apply to the next run you start.
set.saved_but_shadowed: Written, but {count} of them still will not take effect — a later override layer shadows them: {paths}. Change the corresponding data/environment_config.json or environment variable instead.
set.none_written: None of the {count} submitted settings could be written: {paths}
set.not_overridden: This setting was not in the override file to begin with.

pop.state.emotion: 0 = persistently low, 1 = persistently cheerful. Moved by income changes, social feedback and policy shocks.
pop.state.stress: 0 = no stress, 1 = persistently high. Driven by workload, rent and performance pressure.
pop.state.econ_security: How secure they feel about their finances. 0 = could fall over at any moment, 1 = solid ground.
pop.state.city_identity: How much they belong to this city. 0 = strongly alienated, 1 = strongly identified. Usually lower for migrants.
pop.state.policy_sensitivity: How closely they follow policy changes. 0 = barely notice, 1 = highly sensitive.
pop.state.platform_dependence: How dependent they are on online platforms. 0 = diverse offline income, 1 = income and daily life tied to a platform.
pop.state.risk_preference: 0 = strongly risk-averse, 1 = willing to gamble. Affects decisions like starting a business or moving.
pop.state.voice_propensity: Whether they speak up when something is unfair. 0 = stay quiet, 1 = complain or say so publicly.
pop.state.mobility_intent: Whether they want to leave the city. 0 = settling for the long term, 1 = ready to go at any time.
pop.knob.size: How many residents to build. 500 people split into roughly 30–40 cohorts. More people is slower, but the cohort simulation's cost barely grows with headcount.
pop.knob.seed: Where all the random sampling starts. The same parameters with the same seed produce exactly the same people — write the seed down and a colleague gets an identical town. To get different people with the same demographic structure, change only the seed.
pop.knob.name: The output filename prefix — `my_town` gives you my_town_state_init.csv.
pop.knob.median_age: Line everyone up by age; this is the age of the person in the middle. It is squeezed between the child and elderly shares — the reachable range is shown on the right.
pop.knob.share_under_18: The share of the population under 18.
pop.knob.share_over_65: The share of the population aged 65 and over.
pop.knob.migrant_share: The share without local hukou. Migrants usually identify less with the city and are more willing to move on.
pop.knob.mean_size: Average people per household. It trades off against the single-person share — the more one-person households, the lower the ceiling on average size.
pop.knob.share_single_person: The share of households that are one person living alone.
pop.knob.share_multigen: The share of households with three generations (an elder living in). Hard-constrained by the elderly population — without enough elders there cannot be that many such households.
pop.knob.tertiary_rate: The share of adults with tertiary education or above.
pop.knob.employment_rate: The share **of the working-age population (18–64)** who have a job — not of everyone. Children and elders were never counted.
pop.knob.median_monthly: Line up the monthly income of everyone in work; this is the middle one (in yuan).
pop.knob.gini: How wide the income gap is. 0 = everyone earns the same, 1 = one person has all of it. Urban China sits around 0.4.
pop.knob.state_sd: How much people differ inside one cohort. Very small = everyone nearly identical (useful as a control); larger = visible divergence within a cohort.
pop.run.days: How many days to simulate. The longer it runs, the more the differences between cohorts accumulate.
pop.run.budget: How many people per day are pulled out and simulated as full individuals (everyone else just follows their cohort). This is the only cost knob that matters — the cohort layer is nearly free, so total spend is roughly this number times the day count.
pop.run.audit: What share of people to sample each day purely to **measure** how wrong the cohort approximation is — not to make it better. Cutting it saves a little money, but then you cannot see the error at all while it runs.
pop.run.coupling: Lets “neighbours influence each other” show up at the cohort level too. At 0, everyone in a cohort changes identically each day and the social network effectively does not exist — the L2 validation gate will fail. 0.7 is the calibrated value.
pop.run.useLlm: Off substitutes deterministic placeholder text for the model output: the whole run costs nothing, which suits getting the parameters right first. On makes real calls and real charges.
pop.run.provider: Which backend writes the cohort briefings. A local Ollama model costs nothing but is slower; a cloud model is faster and metered.
pop.step1_title: Step 1 · What kind of town is this
pop.step1_lede: Pick a ready-made demographic template first and fine-tune it in the later steps. Each template is self-consistent and runnable as it stands.
pop.field_preset_help: Pick a starting point close to your research scenario. What it actually contains is shown below once selected.
pop.seedbox_body: It decides where the dice-rolling starts. Same parameters plus same seed → the same 500 people, so you and a colleague each get an identical town and the experiment is reproducible. To get different people with the same demographic structure, change only the seed.
pop.step2_title: Step 2 · What these people are like
pop.step2_lede: Drag the sliders to set the demographic features you want. These are population-level shares; the generator fits the correlations between attributes — who earns more, and so on — by itself. When two parameters contradict each other, the panel on the right says immediately which one to change.
pop.generated_hint: Generated. Move a slider above and you will need to regenerate.
pop.generate_hint: Generation takes a second or three and costs nothing in model calls.
pop.gap_note: Some parameters could not be fully met — usually because the conditions you asked for conflict (wanting many three-generation households without enough elders, say). The rows marked red above are the ones that were sacrificed. It does not stop you using the population, but it should be stated in a write-up.
pop.achieved_lede: The table lists each target you set, the value the generated population actually has, and the relative error between them.
pop.chart_pyramid_note: Each bar is a five-year age band — blue left for men, pink right for women — and the longer the bar the more people. Hover for exact counts.
pop.chart_lorenz_note: The dashed line is perfect equality. The further the solid line sits from it, the wider the gap.
pop.chart_household_note: The x-axis is people per household, the y-axis how many households have that many.
pop.chart_social_note: The x-axis is how many social ties a person has, the y-axis how many people have that many. The network is a small world: acquaintances cluster (clustering {clustering} against {random} for random wiring), yet any two people are only {path} hops apart on average.
pop.stat_summary: {label}: mean {mean}, a quarter below {p25}, a quarter above {p75}
pop.roster_lede: Each row is an agent that will take part in the simulation. Click any row to expand its nine state variables. The three files below are exactly what the simulator reads, and can be downloaded as they are.
pop.roster_filter: Filter by name / job / home / hukou
pop.export_hint: Downloaded straight to your machine; nothing is written into the repository. The first two are the files CONFIG["csv_path"] and CONFIG["md_path"] want.
pop.radar_note: The heavy blue line is the mean. The pale band shows where the middle half of people fall — the wider the band, the more the population differs internally. Hover for exact values.
pop.radar_pending: Generate a population in step 2 and the actual state distribution appears here.
pop.step3_lede: Nine variables between 0 and 1 describing each resident's mood, stress, sense of security and so on. What you set here is the **population mean**; each individual is then adjusted by their income, hukou and job.
pop.regen_hint: After moving a slider above, regenerate for it to take effect.
pop.provider_default: Use the default model from the config
pop.coupling_off_warn: Social influence is currently off. Everyone in a cohort changes identically each day and the social network effectively does nothing. This setting suits questions about how the overall distribution moves and how large a policy effect is; it cannot be used to study opinion spread or polarisation (the L2 gate in step 5 will fail).
pop.cost_warn: Real model calls are on, so this run will cost money. Rough estimate: about {briefs} cohort-briefing calls{extra}.
pop.step4_lede: The population is split into cohorts by attribute, and each cohort spends one model call a day on a single briefing; alongside that, a small batch of people per day is simulated in full individual detail. That is what makes a few hundred residents affordable.
pop.slider_budget: People simulated in detail per day
pop.provider_note_on: A local Ollama model costs nothing in API fees.

pop.saving_none: No model calls this run, so there is no cost to compare
pop.tip_population: How many people were in this simulation
pop.tip_cohorts: How many cohorts the attributes split into. Each cohort spends one model call a day
pop.tip_agent_days: How many person-days were pulled out and simulated as full individuals
pop.tip_savings: Simulating every person in full would have taken an estimated {calls} calls
pop.tip_residual: The largest gap between the cohort prediction and what the sampled individuals actually did. Closer to 0 is better; 0 means there was no comparable movement this run
pop.cohorts_note: “Stress mean” is the cohort's average stress level; “stress sd” is how much people inside one cohort differ. It should not fall to 0 — that would mean the cohort has collapsed into a single average person.
pop.file_outside: (the file is outside the repository, so it cannot be opened directly)
pop.written_lede: “Open in a new tab” views a file straight in the browser. These three files are everything the simulator reads — put the first two paths into CONFIG["csv_path"] and CONFIG["md_path"] and you can run an individual simulation on them.

pop.v_intro_p1: Cohort simulation is an approximation: it bundles dozens of people into one cohort and processes them together, which is where the savings come from. The question is what that loses. The validation gate exists to answer it.
pop.v_intro_p2: It runs a controlled experiment: the same people, the same starting point, the same seed, simulated once by cohort and once person by person, and then compares how far the two results diverge. Where they are close, the cohort simulation can be trusted for that kind of question; where they diverge, it cannot.
pop.v_intro_time: It takes anywhere from ten seconds to a minute and costs nothing in model calls.
pop.v_l1_guide: L1 overall distribution: whether the shape of the income and mood distributions matches. Comparing means is not enough — flatten everyone to a single value and the mean can still be right.
pop.v_l2_guide: L2 neighbourhood influence: whether people who are close to each other move together. This is the first thing a cohort simulation loses, because “in the same cohort” and “neighbours of each other” are two different groupings. Essential for any study of opinion spread or polarisation.
pop.v_l3_guide: L3 the margins: whether the share of extreme individuals — someone about to go under, say — survives. The classic failure of any aggregate approximation is getting the middle right while flattening both tails.
pop.v_l4_guide: L4 policy response: apply the same shock (a drop in income, say) and check whether the two simulations agree on the direction and size of the effect, and whether the difference between who is hit hardest survives. Essential for any policy study.
pop.v_watershed: L2 and L4 are the watershed: without them, this cohort simulation cannot be called trustworthy.
pop.v_pass_meaning: The two simulations are close enough here to rely on
pop.v_fail_meaning: They diverge too much here — do not use the cohort simulation for this kind of question
pop.v_inconclusive_meaning: The signal was too weak this run to say either way — it does not count as a pass
pop.v_can_l1: Watch how the overall distribution moves (income, mood, stress)
pop.v_can_l3: Watch the margins (the share in extreme difficulty)
pop.v_can_l4: Run policy experiments (how large an effect a shock has, and who is hit hardest)
pop.v_can_l2: Study anything that travels through the social network: opinion spread, polarisation, word of mouth
pop.v_can_head: ✅ These results can be used to
pop.v_headline_pass: ✅ This cohort simulation holds upAll four checks passed: statistically, its results are not meaningfully different from simulating every person individually. You can draw conclusions from it.
pop.v_headline_fail: ❌ This cohort simulation cannot be fully trusted yetA key check did not pass (see below). {advice}
pop.v_advice_l2: The usual cause is social influence set to 0 — go back to step 4, set it to 0.7 and run again.
pop.v_advice_other: See the note on each item below.
pop.v_technical: Full technical output (for the methods section)

pop.q_l1: The question: do the two simulations give the same distribution shape for income, mood and the rest?
pop.q_l2: The question: do people who are close to each other move together? This is the first thing a cohort simulation loses.
pop.q_l3: The question: has the share of people in the most extreme situations been flattened away?
pop.q_l4: The question: given the same shock, do the two simulations agree on the direction and size of the effect?
pop.moran_example: Take “{metric}”: the individual simulation's co-movement strength is {reference}, the cohort simulation's is {group} — {verdict}
pop.moran_weak: the cohort simulation propagates too weakly — the social network's effect has been shaved off.
pop.moran_strong: the cohort simulation propagates too strongly — neighbourhood influence has been amplified.
pop.l1_detail: The largest gap is on “{metric}”: the two distributions differ by {gap} on average (these metrics live in 0–1, so that is {pct} percentage points). The allowance is {allow} — and that ceiling is not a guess: the individual simulation was first run several times with different seeds to measure its own natural wobble, and that wobble is the yardstick. {verdict}
pop.l1_within: The gap is within the noise.
pop.l4_detail: After the same shock, the individual simulation measured an effect of {reference} and the cohort simulation {group} — {sign}, differing in size by {err}%. The variation in who was affected was retained at {retained}% (too low means the information about who is hit hardest has been flattened away).
pop.l4_opposite: opposite directions, which would lead you to exactly the wrong policy conclusion
pop.l2_detail: This measures whether people close to each other move together. The cohort and individual simulations differ by {z} standard deviations here (the allowance is {tolerance}). That standard deviation is the individual simulation's own natural wobble across seeds, so “one standard deviation off” ≈ “about as different as it is from a rerun of itself”.
pop.l3_detail: Take “{metric}”: the cohort simulation retained {ratio}% of the individual simulation's spread. Near 100% means neither tail was squashed; clearly below it means everyone was pulled toward the middle.
ext.help.tab.currency: How money moves through this world: the macro picture, the firms / government / bank pools, whether the total is conserved, and how wealth is distributed. You can also change the economic rules here, or apply one intervention to the run in progress.
ext.help.tab.environment: What happened in the world each day: weather, economic news, policy, technology. These events enter every resident's situation for that day and move their mood and their schedule.
ext.help.tab.services: Everywhere the simulation dials out to: the external environment service, the multi-machine relay, news sources, and which model is used. You can check whether each is reachable, and change it.
ext.help.tile.phase: The economy's four seasons: expansion → peak → contraction → trough, round and round. Raise and layoff chances differ by phase.
ext.help.tile.inflation: How much prices rise each year. Note it acts only on the spending side — wages do not follow, so over a long run residents can afford steadily less.
ext.help.tile.unemployment: A macro business-climate indicator. It does not actually cost anyone their job — what drives layoffs is each phase's layoff chance. Read it as the number the news reports.
ext.help.tile.price_index: The cumulative price index: it starts at 1.0 and compounds by the daily inflation. 1.05 means things now cost 5% more than at the opening.
ext.help.tile.money_total: The total money in this world: every resident's accounts plus the three pools. Unless you inject some yourself, it should never change.
ext.help.tile.drift: Conservation drift: how far today's total money is from the opening total. Anything other than 0 is a bug — money should only change hands, never appear or vanish.
ext.help.tile.gini: The wealth gap: 0 = everyone equal, 1 = one person has it all. China sits around 0.47. With only one resident it cannot be computed and shows “—”.
ext.help.tile.indebted: How many people owe money — a bank credit line or a loan from a friend — and have not repaid it.
ext.help.block.sectors: Residents spend and earn, and there has to be a counterparty. The firms pool pays wages and takes revenue; the government pool collects tax and pays medical cover; the bank pool handles deposits, loans and investment results. A negative pool is normal — a negative firms pool just means residents as a whole are saving.
ext.help.block.conservation: The daily total money, plotted. Ideally a flat line: money only changes hands between residents and the three pools, so the total holds.
ext.help.block.ledger: What all residents earned and spent each day. Spending persistently above income means they are living off savings.
ext.help.block.wealth: Only money that can be spent now (current account + savings + investments). The housing fund is counted separately — it cannot be withdrawn, so it does not belong in “how much money they have”.
ext.help.block.queue: An intervention you queue is written to a file that a running simulation picks up at each day boundary. With nothing running, it waits until the next run starts.
ext.help.iv.form: This changes the run in progress. Blank fields are left alone. To change the next run's starting conditions, use “Config” below.
ext.help.iv.phase: Switch the economy straight to a phase — into a downturn immediately, say.
ext.help.iv.inflation: Sets the value outright, not as an increment. Anything wild is pulled back into a sane range (0.1%–15%).
ext.help.iv.unemployment: Sets the value outright, not as an increment. Range 2%–20%.
ext.help.iv.sector: This is how much to add or remove, not what to set it to. 50000 puts 50,000 into the pool; -50000 takes it out. That is printing or destroying money, and the system books it honestly rather than treating it as a leak.
ext.help.iv.day: Which day it takes effect. Blank means the next one.
ext.help.iv.note: A note for yourself. It goes into the history so you can tell later what this one was for.
ext.help.cfg.card: What you change here is the rules for the next run; the one in progress is unaffected. After saving you are told what was actually written.
ext.help.env.latest_day: How far the environment has been generated.
ext.help.env.day_count: How many days of environment exist in total.
ext.help.env.ticks: Beyond the day's opening environment, how many intraday shocks turned up.
ext.help.env.severity: The mean severity of every event, 0–1. A high overall figure means the world has been eventful lately.
ext.help.env.sev_bar: How severe this event is, 0–1. Above 0.6 it turns red. A severe event markedly raises the chance a resident changes plans that day.
ext.help.env.tags: Which aspects of residents it touches — travel, stress, employment and so on.
ext.help.env.type: The four sources an event comes from: natural (weather), economic, policy, technology.
ext.help.svc.probe: Pressing this really does request that address once to see whether it is alive. Nothing probes in the background otherwise.
ext.help.svc.status: “up” = fine; “down” = unreachable; “error” = reached but the response was wrong; “off” = disabled in the config, so no request was made at all.
ext.help.svc.llm: The provider list is read-only (it carries keys, which are not exposed in the browser). What you can change is who does what — sending a simple job like schedule drafting to a cheap local model, say.
ext.help.svc.news: The external news residents read. The cache exists so it need not be fetched over the network every time.
ext.help.economy.routing: Part of what a resident spends in a shop passes through the firms pool to whichever resident works there, as income; rent goes to a landlord resident. This is what lets money circulate between residents at all, and what lets a wealth gap evolve on its own.
ext.help.economy.social_insurance.unempl: The employee's unemployment-insurance contribution rate, deducted from wages. Default 0.5%.
ext.help.economy.macro.enabled: Off means no economic cycle: no expansion or downturn, and inflation stops moving.
ext.help.llm.routing: Which task uses which model. “Default model” is the fallback; “per-task” assigns an individual task its own.
ext.help.default: Every task without its own assignment uses this model.
ext.help.enabled: Off takes this subsystem out of the simulation entirely.
ext.help.economy: The rules of the whole economy. Changing these changes this world's economic system, from the next run on.
ext.help.output_dir: Which directory this module writes its result files to.
ext.help.tax: Personal income tax. China's actual 2024 rules: everything above the exemption is taxed across seven progressive bands.
ext.help.monthly_exemption: Monthly income below this is untaxed. China currently uses ¥5,000. Raising it cuts everyone's tax.
ext.help.default_special_deduction: The default allowance for special deductions (mortgage, children's education, elder support) subtracted before tax is computed.
ext.help.brackets: The rate table; each row is [upper bound of this band, rate, quick deduction]. The last row's bound is Infinity. Getting it wrong miscomputes everyone's tax, so change the numbers within the existing shape.
ext.help.social_insurance: The employee's share of the five insurances and the housing fund, deducted monthly from wages. Raising it lowers take-home pay.
ext.help.pension_rate: The employee's pension contribution rate, default 8%.
ext.help.medical_rate: The employee's medical insurance rate, default 2%.
ext.help.housing_fund_rate: The employee's housing-fund rate. The money is not gone — it goes into the housing-fund account — but it cannot be spent day to day.
ext.help.housing_fund_employer_rate: The employer's housing-fund contribution, which also lands in your account: effectively hidden income.
ext.help.base_cap: Contribution base ceiling: however high the wage, social insurance is computed on at most this.
ext.help.base_floor: Contribution base floor: however low the wage, social insurance is computed on at least this.
ext.help.spending: How residents spend: how much, and on what.
ext.help.engel_curve: The Engel curve; each row is [monthly income, food share, savings rate]. Poorer people spend a larger share on food and save little; richer people the reverse. It is one of economics' most repeatedly confirmed regularities.
ext.help.budget_template: How the monthly budget splits across the eight categories (food, housing, transport, clothing, leisure, education, medical, other). The shares should sum to 1.
ext.help.income_elasticity: Which category grows faster as income rises. Above 1 = a luxury (income doubles, this grows more); below 1 = a necessity.
ext.help.daily_variance: How much daily spending wobbles at random, so no two days are identical.
ext.help.investment: How residents invest, and how the market moves.
ext.help.asset_returns: [annual mean return, volatility] for each of the three asset classes. Deposits are steady but small; equities large but jumpy.
ext.help.portfolio_profiles: How conservative / moderate / aggressive people each split their money across deposits, funds and equities.
ext.help.market_correlation: Whether a crash hits everyone at once. 0 = each on their own, 1 = perfectly in lockstep. Lower it and a market-wide collapse can no longer happen.
ext.help.auto_save_enabled: When the current account exceeds the buffer months, the surplus moves automatically into savings and investments.
ext.help.checking_buffer_months: How many months of spending to keep in the current account as emergency money; only the excess is invested.
ext.help.credit: How much residents can borrow when short, and how expensive it is.
ext.help.credit_limit_months: The credit limit as a multiple of monthly pay. Larger means people can overdraw further.
ext.help.annual_interest_rate: The annual rate on an overdraft, default 18% — close to a real credit card.
ext.help.hardship_liquidity_months: When their money will not last this many months, residents start cutting non-essential spending.
ext.help.min_spend_factor: The floor share they spend however tight things get, so nobody starves.
ext.help.macro: The wider economy: how the cycle turns, how high inflation and unemployment run, and how each industry is doing.
ext.help.initial_inflation_rate: The opening inflation rate. Raise it to model a high-inflation society.
ext.help.initial_unemployment_rate: The opening unemployment rate (a business-climate indicator only).
ext.help.cycle_phase_duration_days: How many days each phase lasts, drawn at random between [shortest, longest]. Smaller means more frequent cycles.
ext.help.phases: The order the four phases rotate in.
ext.help.phase_effects: What each phase actually does to residents: income, spending, and the chances of a layoff or a raise. What actually costs someone their job is layoff_risk here.
ext.help.income_mult: The income multiplier in this phase. 0.9 = a 10% across-the-board pay cut.
ext.help.expense_mult: The spending multiplier in this phase.
ext.help.layoff_risk: The chance per resident per day of being laid off in this phase. 0.025 looks small, but over a few dozen days it adds up considerably.
ext.help.raise_chance: The chance per resident per day of a raise in this phase.
ext.help.industry_conditions: How each industry is doing, with 1.0 as normal. At 0.7 the industry is depressed and its workers' incomes suffer.
ext.help.expansion: Good times: income rising, few layoffs, raises easy to come by.
ext.help.peak: Overheating: income at its highest, but so are prices, and layoffs begin to pick up.
ext.help.contraction: Downturn: income falling, spending still rising, layoffs clearly up.
ext.help.trough: The bottom: income lowest and layoffs worst, but prices easing. Get through it and expansion begins again.
ext.help.conservative: How a conservative investor splits deposits / funds / equities. The three should sum to 1.
ext.help.moderate: How a moderate investor splits deposits / funds / equities. The three should sum to 1.
ext.help.aggressive: How an aggressive investor splits deposits / funds / equities. The three should sum to 1.
ext.help.inheritance_hukou_bonus: How the chance of family money differs by hukou. Positive = more likely to have some, negative = less.
ext.help.shocks: Accidents that land on an individual: layoffs, raises, serious illness, the year-end bonus.
ext.help.layoff_base_prob: The background layoff chance, independent of the cycle.
ext.help.raise_base_prob: The background raise chance, independent of the cycle.
ext.help.medical_emergency_prob: The chance per resident per day of a serious illness. Insurance covers most of it; the rest comes out of pocket.
ext.help.medical_cost_range: The cost range of a serious illness, [least, most].
ext.help.year_end_bonus_enabled: Whether a year-end bonus is paid.
ext.help.year_end_bonus_months: How many months' wages the year-end bonus is worth.
ext.help.merchant_labor_share: What share of money spent in a shop passes to whoever works there, as income. Raising it moves money between residents faster.
ext.help.landlord_share: What share of rent actually reaches a landlord resident's pocket.
ext.help.landlord_keywords: Who counts as a landlord is recognised from these words in their job description.
ext.help.friend_loans: Borrowing from acquaintances when short. It travels the social network — the closer the tie, the likelier the loan.
ext.help.max_outstanding_months: The most months of spending one may owe friends.
ext.help.lender_buffer_months: How many months of their own spending a lender keeps back before agreeing to lend.
ext.help.willingness_factor: Overall willingness to lend. Lower it and nobody is very keen.
ext.help.sectors: The three pools' opening balances. All 0 by default, with the money entirely in residents' hands.
ext.help.initial_firms_balance: How much the firms pool opens with.
ext.help.initial_government_balance: How much the government pool opens with. Raising it is the treasury having reserves.
ext.help.initial_bank_balance: How much the bank pool opens with.
ext.help.inheritance_enabled: Some residents start with family money (an inheritance or parental help). It is one of the main sources of the opening wealth gap.
ext.help.inheritance_base_probability: What share of residents receive help from family.
ext.help.income_volatility: How much daily income wobbles at random.
ext.help.min_hourly_income: The floor on hourly pay; it never goes below this whatever happens.
ext.help.daily_utilities_cost: The fixed daily cost of water, power and gas.
ext.help.expense_ranges: The cost range, [least, most], when each kind of behaviour fires.
ext.help.external_environment: The module that generates the four kinds of daily event: weather, economic, policy, technology.
ext.help.seed: The random seed. The same number gives the same world; a different one is a different history.
ext.help.max_events_per_tick: The most events thrown at once, so the feed is not flooded.
ext.help.generator: Whether events are written by a model or drawn by rule from the preset copy.
ext.help.mode: `llm` = the model invents them, with more flair and a real cost; anything else uses the preset pools below, free.
ext.help.history_days: How many previous days the model sees when writing today's events, so the story stays coherent.
ext.help.description: This city's background setting, given to the model as the basis for its writing.
ext.help.daily_weather_chance: The chance of generating a weather event on a given day.
ext.help.extreme_chance: The chance of extreme weather — a downpour, a thunderstorm.
ext.help.weather_states: The weight of each weather state; larger is more common.
ext.help.extreme_events: The copy pool for extreme weather.
ext.help.daily_market_volatility: How much the market moves each day.
ext.help.market_news_threshold_pct: A move is only reported once it passes this percentage, so there is no daily filler.
ext.help.macro_event_chance: The chance of one macroeconomic news item per day.
ext.help.macro_events: The copy pool for macro news.
ext.help.daily_policy_chance: The chance of one policy per day.
ext.help.daily_tech_chance: The chance of one technology item per day.
ext.help.intraday: Shocks that turn up during the day, as opposed to the batch settled at each morning.
ext.help.environment: The older environment events, kept for compatibility. Normally left alone.
ext.help.policy_events: Policy shocks scheduled in advance: name the day, the time and what happens, and it fires on cue. Use this for a policy experiment — it is far more reliable than tuning probabilities.
ext.help.external_environment_service: Move environment generation to another process or another machine. Off generates it in this process.
ext.help.timeout: How many seconds to wait for a response before giving up.
ext.help.fallback_to_empty: When the other end is down, carry on as if nothing happened today (recommended) or fail outright.
ext.help.environment_server: The listen settings when this machine is the environment server. Restart that service process after changing them.
ext.help.host: Which interface to listen on. 0.0.0.0 lets other machines connect.
ext.help.external_rag: The mechanism that feeds real outside information into residents' memories.
ext.help.top_k: How many of the most relevant items each retrieval returns.
ext.help.bootstrap: Inject a batch of background information into every resident at the opening.
ext.help.runtime_absorb: Keep absorbing new information each day during the run (off by default; on is slower and costlier).
ext.help.news: The real news sources residents read.
ext.help.use_cache_first: Prefer the local cache over fetching over the network every time — faster, and less likely to get blocked by a site.
ext.help.daily_chance: The chance a resident reads the news on a given day.
ext.help.max_reads_per_day: The most items one resident may read per day, so nobody reads all day.
ext.help.info_seek: Residents searching the web themselves, as opposed to passively reading news. The stressed and the curious search more often.
ext.help.distributed: Several machines running one world between them, each owning some of the residents.
ext.help.relay: Where the relay server is, when this machine is a client.
ext.help.server: The listen settings when this machine is the relay server.
ext.help.send_probability: The chance per step of sending a message to a peer.
ext.help.tasks: Assign an individual task its own model — sending schedule drafting to a cheap local one, say.
ext.not_json: The server did not return JSON (HTTP {status})
ext.too_few_points: Not enough data points — run a simulation and come back.
ext.cons_drift: The conservation audit found drift: money appeared or vanished somewhere. That is usually a bug, not a setting.
ext.cons_ok: The conservation audit passed: the system total matched the opening stock every day.
ext.cons_none: No conservation audit data yet — a run generates it.
ext.iv_none_applied: No intervention has been applied yet.
ext.currency_lede: Read from the most recent run's output ({path}). The macro state advances daily with the cycle, and money circulates between agents and the firms / government / bank pools.
ext.injected_total: of which: injected by hand, cumulative
ext.wealth_lede: Measured as liquid assets (current account + savings + investments); the housing fund is listed separately.
ext.w_median_help: Half have more, half have less. The further it sits from the mean, the more skewed the distribution.
ext.w_fund_help: The money really is theirs, but it cannot be withdrawn and spent day to day, so it is not counted in the liquid assets above.
ext.w_gini_na: — (fewer than 2 residents, or a total of 0)
ext.queue_lede: An intervention submitted on the right is written to {path}, and a running simulation consumes it at each day boundary. With nothing running, it waits until the next run starts.
ext.iv_form_title: Intervene in the running money system
ext.iv_form_lede: Blank fields are left alone. A pool balance is a delta (positive injects, negative withdraws); an injection also raises the conservation baseline, so the audit does not misreport it as a leak.
ext.cfg_currency_hint: This changes the next run's starting conditions (tax rates, social insurance, the Engel curve, the macro cycle, shock probabilities …). The run in progress is unaffected.
ext.env_empty: No timeline.jsonl yet. After a run, the environment events generated each day appear here.
ext.env_overview_lede: The environment generator throws four kinds of event each day — natural, economic, policy, technology — into every agent's situation for that day. Read from {path}
ext.cfg_env_hint: These control the environment generator: the daily probability of each event kind, the weather weights, the copy pools, and the policy shocks scheduled in policy_events. Changes apply to the next run.
ext.svc_lede: Where the simulation dials out: the external environment service and the distributed relay. The button below probes them once, now.
ext.llm_lede: The available models come from `providers` in the config (keys are neither exposed nor editable here). Routing decides which task uses which model.
ext.cfg_svc_hint: The external environment service address, the distributed relay, external information injection, news sources and LLM routing. Changes apply to the next run; a server process has to be restarted by hand.
ext.json_errors: {count} JSON fields cannot be parsed — fix them before saving: {paths}
ext.confirm_switch: There are unsaved config changes and switching will lose them. Continue?
sd.new_mode_hint: New resident: fill in identity and state, then press Save to create
sd.pick_resident: Pick a resident, or create a new one.
sd.seed_job_ph: e.g. junior software engineer, leaves the office 9–10pm
sd.seed_personality_ph: introverted and analytical, anxious around review season…
sd.identity_note: Who this digital resident is. These fields are written to the state CSV and the profile.
sd.name: Name
sd.profile_empty: No profile text yet — press Edit to start writing.
sd.profile_write_back: Written back to the profile file on confirm
sd.profile_edit_hint: Edit the Markdown source, then confirm to write
sd.b5hint.rewrite.flip: The paragraph was written from the opposite pole; the sentences for this trait have to be rewritten
sd.b5hint.rewrite.drift: The paragraph covers this trait, but the score has moved well away from the pole it describes
sd.b5hint.now_missing: It was not distinct before, so it never made it into the paragraph; now it is — the paragraph is missing this trait
sd.b5hint.now_moot: The paragraph covers this trait but it is no longer distinct — the paragraph describes a leaning that no longer exists
sd.b5hint.unknown: There is no record of which scores the paragraph was written from, so it cannot be compared
sd.big5_unsaved: A new resident needs to be saved before it has a personality-score row.
sd.big5_no_para: This resident's profile has no “personality and behavioural leanings” paragraph yet.
sd.big5_note: z scores; 0 is the population mean, and |z| ≥ {floor} counts as distinct for this person. These are independent of the nine state variables above — the scores were sampled first and the paragraph written from them, not inferred from it. Changes are written to {file} and take effect on the next run.
sd.b5_para_manual: Edited by hand; this panel never rewrites it
sd.b5_para_note: This paragraph was written from the scores above. Change the scores without changing it and the rule channel acts on the new scores while the prompt still describes the old person — which is exactly what the flagged traits above mean.
sd.b5_para_where: The paragraph is edited under Narrative profile in step 1
sd.big5_saved: Personality scores written to data/agents_big5.csv (effective next run)
sd.state_note: Nine normalized [0,1] state variables — GAWorld's “personality and inner state”. Dragging updates the radar live; press Confirm changes to write them to the CSV and the profile.
sd.growth_empty: No growth record yet — derived by gaworld/interests.py once the simulation has run.
sd.practiced: {minutes} min total · {streak}-day streak · last practised on day {day}
sd.caps_empty: No capability profile yet — read from output/work/capabilities.json once the simulation has run.
sd.private_skills_empty: No private skills yet — distilled from experience during a run.
sd.cog_note: A transparent index (60–140) derived from skills / growth / memory / external knowledge. Not a measured IQ.
sd.skills_note: Capability profile and skills come from simulation output; interests and growth are read live from the agent's growth record (level / practice minutes / streak).
sd.mem_pick_node: Click a node in the graph to read that memory in full.
sd.mem_note: Layered memory — long-term / habits / intentions / schedule — read from output/memory. It accumulates as the simulation runs, and can also be written by hand here.
sd.mem_has_traces: This resident already has memory traces.
sd.mem_none_yet: No memories yet — this fills in once the simulation has run, or add them by hand below.
sd.mem_hidden: The graph shows at most 10 nodes per kind; {n} more are in the zoomed view.
sd.mem_add_ph: e.g. last month a letting agent overcharged them in Wulin Subdistrict, and they have been wary of agents since.
sd.mem_add_hint: Long-term memories are written straight into agent_{id}.json; RAG entries get an [额外信息 | 来源:manual] prefix and are indexed too when a vector store exists.
sd.mem_habit_empty: No habits yet — they harden out of repeated behaviour during a run.
sd.save_first_memory: Save the resident before adding memories
sd.rag_empty: No externally injected knowledge yet — [额外信息] memories are seeded by external_rag or written by retrieval at run time.
sd.partner_agent_note: Applies both ways: the other resident's family changes too and the two share one dwelling; whoever was paired with them falls back to an off-stage spouse.
sd.partner_none_note: Pinned to no partner — no spouse is generated even when the sampled marital status is married.
sd.partner_auto_note: Decided automatically from marital status and the pairing rules.
sd.family_unsaved: Save the new resident before editing their family.
sd.family_note: Households are regenerated at the start of every run from Config → Families and households. Edits here are saved as overrides in {file}; they persist across runs and take precedence over the sampled result.
sd.children_hint: Generated from the fertility knobs. Tick this to specify each child exactly.
sd.elders_hint: Generated from the co-residence rules. Tick this to specify which elders live here.
sd.family_reset_done: Reverted to generated; effective next run
sd.family_save_done: Family settings saved; effective next run
sd.social_new: Relationship edges appear once the new resident is saved and a simulation has run.
sd.social_loaded: {n} real relationship edges loaded (output/memory); edit them directly.
sd.social_no_file: No relationship file yet — anything added here creates agent_{id}_relationships.json.
sd.social_new_locked: Relationships cannot be edited while creating a resident.
sd.social_evolves: Network density, homophily and the rest evolve during a run.
sd.rel_name_required: Give every relationship a name first
sd.goals_empty: No goal record yet — seeded from the profile by gaworld/goals.py once the simulation has run, or written from this dashboard.
sd.behavior_note: The state dimensions that drive behaviour: mobility, expression, risk, platform lock-in, policy sensitivity.
sd.goals_new_note: Once the new resident is saved, goals are seeded from the profile by gaworld/goals.py and can be edited back here.
sd.goals_edit_note: Goals are editable here; Save goals writes goals.json. A run advances them daily and reviews them weekly.
sd.finance_empty: Generated from the economy state under output/memory once the simulation has run; savings and the rest are editable then.
sd.finance_no_state: This resident has no live agent_{id}_economy.json yet — run the simulation once and it becomes editable.
sd.finance_note: Written to agent_{id}_economy.json — read the next time the simulation starts in stateful mode. Balance = current + savings + investments (housing fund excluded).
sd.fin_saved: Finance saved to the economy state
sd.review_create_note: Confirming creates the new resident (writes the CSV + profile).
sd.review_save_note: Confirming saves the changes, ready to run.
sd.interview_label: Ask a question (calls the LLM; can be slow)
sd.interview_ph: e.g. what do you make of the recent hukou policy?
sd.run_with_resident: Run a simulation with this resident
sd.oc_none: No OpenClaw traffic seen on the relay (scripts/openclaw_bridge.py connects it).
sd.run_started: Simulation started with resident #{id} (see the console for logs)
sd.interview_running: Interviewing (this can take tens of seconds)…
sim.city_hint: Which city this run happens in: it decides the map, the environment events, the background prompt and the resident roster. "Default world" is the original Hangzhou data under data/. Create cities in the Cities tab. Switching city also switches the roster, so Agent IDs must fall within the new city's population.
city.map_empty: This city has no map yet
city.knowledge_note: The city's industries and labour market. It feeds cognition prompts, steers which skills residents learn, biases local pay by industry, and is written into every resident's retrievable memory.
city.knowledge_empty: No knowledge yet. Use "Research online", or "Estimate from map" to derive it from the existing map.
survey.meta_description: GAWorld group interview: ask one question set to many agents across cities, tally multiple-choice and yes/no answers, export the full Markdown document
survey.headline: Ask a crowd the same question
survey.sub: Pick respondents across cities (individual residents or cohort agents) → write questions (open / multiple-choice / yes-no, with images and URLs) → read the tallies and breakdowns → ask follow-ups → download the full document.
survey.step1_hint: Pick respondents across cities: individual residents, or cohort agents that answer for a whole group
survey.step2_hint: Write the questions, pick each one's type, and attach an image or a URL
survey.step3_hint: Summary, option tallies, distributions by city / age / hukou, and every answer verbatim
survey.basket_hint: A cohort agent speaks for all its members — far cheaper than interviewing them one by one, at the cost of individual voices.
survey.cost_hint: Every question to every respondent is one model call — that is where the continuity comes from: answering question 4, they can see their own answer to question 1.
survey.no_population: These cities have no residents yet — generate some in Cities or Population first.
survey.cohorts_head: Cohort agents (one answer stands for the whole group)
survey.caption_ph: Caption (used instead of the picture when the model cannot see images)
survey.url_ph: Attach a URL (its article text goes into the question)
survey.context_label: Shared background (optional, applies to every question)
survey.context_ph: e.g. The city plans to extend Line 5 westwards
survey.pick_first: No respondents yet — go back to step 1.
survey.no_results: No results yet. Start an interview in step 2.
survey.result_meta: {respondents} respondents ({individuals} individual, {cohorts} cohort), standing for {people} people; {questions} questions over {rounds} round(s).
survey.unparsed: could not be parsed into this question's shape; excluded from the tally
survey.cov_unparsed: {n} did not follow the question's format and are excluded from the tally
pd.title: Distil a real person
pd.note: Enter a name or a URL. GAWorld searches public sources, reads the pages, and distils an evidence-backed portrait: a biography plus mental models, decision heuristics, expression style and the limits of the portrait. Only what the search returned is used; gaps are left explicitly blank.
pd.gaps: Left blank for lack of sources
pd.no_models: The material does not support any model that recurs across domains.
pd.no_heuristics: No reusable decision rule was distilled.
pd.need_subject: Enter a name or a URL.
pd.done: Done — review the evidence and the limits before deploying.
pd.no_big5: (Big Five not written: seed file missing)
pd.discard_ask: Delete this portrait and its research material? Residents already deployed are unaffected.
sd.persona_filled: Filled the form with the distilled portrait of {name} — review each step, then save.
